rules.statement: In a test project, cover each public factory or overload with a success-path test that shows its input is actually applied, and with null-argument tests that assert the ArgumentNullException's ParamName for each guard.
rules.why: If an overload accepts its input but drops its values, or a null guard is removed, tests that only cover a failure path still pass.
rules.check: New public overloads or ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull guards whose tests only cover an error case, or have no test passing null and asserting ParamName.

rules.statement: In a test project, when code promises an ordering (such as stopping services in reverse registration order), add a test that records the order and asserts it, rather than test doubles that only count calls.
rules.why: Doubles that only count calls let the order change without any test failing.
rules.check: A documented or ADR-stated ordering whose test doubles only count invocations and no test asserts the sequence.

rules.statement: In a test project, when a builder enables ServiceProviderOptions such as ValidateOnBuild or ValidateScopes, add a test that registers a service with an unresolvable dependency and asserts that the build fails with the AggregateException ValidateOnBuild raises, holding an InvalidOperationException that names the dependency.
rules.why: Without that test, dropping the provider options would let a broken composition build and fail only on first use.
rules.check: BuildServiceProvider calls with ValidateOnBuild/ValidateScopes and no test that exercises a missing dependency.

rules.statement: In a test project, when a test expects a common exception type such as InvalidOperationException from a specific guard, capture the exception and assert something that identifies that guard, such as part of its message, instead of checking the type alone.
rules.why: Any other exception of the same type from the call would pass, so the test wouldn't prove the intended guard threw.
rules.check: Assert.Throws<InvalidOperationException> (or similar) whose result isn't inspected, where the call could throw that type for more than one reason.

rules.statement: In a test project, make each test check only the single behavior its name states, and split a test that asserts several outcomes (such as stopping, disposing and the thrown exception) into separate tests.
rules.why: When a multi-behavior test fails, its name doesn't say which behavior broke, and the assertions after the failing one don't run.
rules.check: Tests whose assertions cover outcomes the test name leaves out, or names that join several outcomes with 'And'.

rules.statement: In a test project, declare a literal value that a test double and an assertion both use as a single const on the double, and reference it in both places instead of repeating the literal.
rules.why: Duplicated literals can drift apart, and the test would then fail for a reason unrelated to the behavior.
rules.check: The same string or number literal appearing both in a stub's member and in an assertion against it.

rules.statement: Give private helpers, constructors, fields and properties a /// summary (with <param> tags on methods) that states non-obvious behavior such as ordering and which exceptions they throw, instead of a plain // comment or no comment.
rules.why: Otherwise nothing at the helper itself documents contracts such as reverse-order stopping or merging failures into an AggregateException.
rules.check: Private members in a change that have no /// summary, or only a // comment, especially helpers with ordering or exception semantics.

rules.statement: Create a collection that is usually empty, such as a list of caught failures, lazily on first use (for example `List<Exception>? failures = null; (failures ??= []).Add(ex)`) instead of allocating it on every call.
rules.why: Allocating it up front costs every call an allocation it usually doesn't need.
rules.check: `new List<...>()` created at the start of a method only to collect rare items such as exceptions in a catch block.
